Call a nonzero unital complex \(C^*\)-algebra \(M\) a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor if its center is \(\mathbb C1\), every subset \(S\subseteq M\) has right annihilator
\[
\{x\in M:sx=0\text{ for every }s\in S\}=pM
\]
for some projection \(p=p^*=p^2\), and every \(v\in M\) satisfying \(v^*v=1\) also satisfies \(vv^*=1\).

A quasitrace on a unital \(C^*\)-algebra \(A\) is a map \(q:A\to\mathbb C\) that is complex-linear on each abelian \(C^*\)-subalgebra and satisfies
\[
q(x^*x)=q(xx^*)\geq0,\qquad q(h+ik)=q(h)+iq(k)
\]
for every \(x\in A\) and self-adjoint \(h,k\in A\). It is a \(2\)-quasitrace if there is a quasitrace \(q_2\) on the matrix algebra \(M_2(A)\) such that \(q_2(\operatorname{diag}(x,0))=q(x)\) for every \(x\in A\). It is normalized if \(q(1)=1\), and faithful if \(q(x^*x)=0\) implies \(x=0\).

Let \(\mathcal G\) be the set of all real numbers \(\eta>0\) for which there exist a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor \(M\), a faithful normalized \(2\)-quasitrace \(\tau\) on \(M\), and self-adjoint elements \(a_0,a_1,\ldots\in M\) satisfying
\[
0\leq a_n\leq a_{n+1}\leq1,
\qquad
\tau(a_{n+1}-a_n)=\eta
\qquad(n=0,1,2,\ldots),
\]
such that \((a_n)\) has no least upper bound in \(M_{\mathrm{sa}}=\{x\in M:x=x^*\}\). Here \(x\leq y\) means that \(y-x\) is positive in the \(C^*\)-algebra order.

Determine \(\mathcal G\) exactly.

My previous answer was not justified: the monotone-completeness theorem I invoked is not available under these hypotheses.

In fact, **even deciding whether \(\mathcal G\) is empty is equivalent to an unresolved regularity question for finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factors**. The precise equivalence is
\[
\boxed{\quad
\mathcal G=\varnothing
\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\text{every finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor is monotone sequentially complete}.
\quad}
\]
Here monotone sequential completeness means that every norm-bounded increasing sequence of self-adjoint elements has a least upper bound in the self-adjoint part.

The nontrivial point is that the requirement of *constant positive quasitrace increments* does not avoid that open problem. Here is why.

### From a missing supremum to constant increments

We use two standard facts about finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factors:

* They possess a canonical faithful normalized \(2\)-quasitrace.
* Their norm-bounded sets are complete for the quasitrace metric
  \[
  d_\tau(x,y)=\tau\bigl((x-y)^*(x-y)\bigr)^{1/3}.
  \]
  On bounded sets, the positive cone is closed for this metric.

Consequently, if a bounded increasing sequence is \(d_\tau\)-Cauchy, its metric limit is its least upper bound.

Suppose, therefore, that a finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor has an increasing sequence with no least upper bound. After an affine rescaling, write it as
\[
0\le b_0\le b_1\le\cdots\le1.
\]
It cannot be \(d_\tau\)-Cauchy. Since
\[
0\le b_m-b_n\le1,
\qquad
\tau((b_m-b_n)^2)\le\tau(b_m-b_n),
\]
and a \(2\)-quasitrace is order-preserving, it follows that
\[
\delta:=\inf_n\sup_{m\ge n}\tau(b_m-b_n)>0.
\]

Interpolate linearly between successive terms:
\[
b(n+s)=(1-s)b_n+s b_{n+1}\qquad(0\le s\le1).
\]
This gives a norm-continuous increasing path.

Fix \(0<\eta<\delta\). Starting at \(t_0=0\), choose successively \(t_{j+1}>t_j\) such that
\[
\tau\bigl(b(t_{j+1})-b(t_j)\bigr)=\eta.
\]
Such a choice exists by continuity: the expression starts at zero and eventually exceeds \(\eta\), by the definition of \(\delta\).

Moreover, \(t_j\to\infty\). Otherwise norm-continuity on a compact interval would force
\(\tau(b(t_{j+1})-b(t_j))\to0\), contradicting its constant value \(\eta\).

Thus
\[
a_j=b(t_j)
\]
is cofinal with \((b_n)\). The two sequences have exactly the same upper bounds, so \((a_j)\) has no least upper bound. It satisfies all the requirements defining \(\eta\in\mathcal G\).

This proves that failure of monotone sequential completeness produces elements of \(\mathcal G\). The converse is immediate from its definition.

\[
\mathcal G\subset(0,1),
\qquad
\eta\in\mathcal G,\ 0<\eta'\le\eta
\ \Longrightarrow\ \eta'\in\mathcal G.
\]
The second follows by scaling a witnessing sequence. For the first, increments are bounded by \(1\); equality \(\tau(a_{n+1}-a_n)=1\), together with faithfulness, would force \(a_{n+1}-a_n=1\), which cannot occur repeatedly inside \([0,1]\).

But an unconditional exact determination would, in particular, resolve the open monotone sequential completeness question above. Accordingly, the earlier unconditional assertion \(\mathcal G=\varnothing\) must be replaced by this dependence on that unresolved regularity property.

## Overall result

The team **did not prove \(\mathcal G=\varnothing\)**. They proved the tracial, commuting, and finite-dimensional cases, developed several useful reductions and auxiliary lemmas, and found counterexamples to proposed shortcuts. **Nothing they found contradicts the prescribed answer.** The unresolved case is a genuinely noncommuting sequence in a diffuse finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factor with a possibly nonlinear quasitrace.

Python checked finite algebraic identities and matrix examples—not the missing infinite-dimensional theorem.

## Main proved reductions

Write
\[
b_n=a_{n+1}-a_n.
\]
Then
\[
b_n\ge0,\qquad \sum_{n<N}b_n=a_N-a_0\le1,\qquad \tau(b_n)=\eta.
\]
Thus a sufficient, stronger statement would be **quasitracial exhaustion**: bounded positive partial sums force \(\tau(b_n)\to0\). They did not prove it. In particular, one cannot telescope quasitrace values as though \(\tau\) were linear.

For \(0<\eta\le1\), spectral projections
\[
p_n=1_{(\eta/2,1]}(b_n)
\]
satisfy
\[
\tau(p_n)\ge\frac{\eta}{2-\eta}\ge\frac\eta2,
\qquad
\sum_{n<N}p_n\le\frac2\eta\,1.
\]
The first inequality follows from
\(b_n\le(\eta/2)(1-p_n)+p_n\); the second from
\(b_n\ge(\eta/2)p_n\).
This reduces exhaustion to excluding an infinite **projection Bessel family** with uniformly positive dimension. Projection-lattice finiteness alone did not supply that exclusion.

They also proved sign/contraction bounds for positive partial sums, including
\[
\left\|\sum_i\varepsilon_i b_i\right\|\le1
\quad(\varepsilon_i=\pm1).
\]
No usable quasitracial cotype estimate followed.

## Complete special cases

If \(\tau\) is a trace on a subalgebra containing the sequence, then
\[
N\eta=\tau(a_N-a_0)\le1,
\]
a contradiction for sufficiently large \(N\). This covers commuting sequences.

For \(M=M_d(\mathbb C)\), the quasitrace axioms imply unitary invariance; abelian additivity then gives \(\tau(p)=\operatorname{rank}(p)/d\). Spectral decomposition shows \(\tau=\operatorname{Tr}/d\), so the same argument excludes all type-I finite factors.

## Connection with monotone sequential completeness

A substantial contribution was **constant-gap interpolation preserving the entire upper-bound set**.

Starting from a bounded increasing positive sequence \(s_n\) with uniform quasitracial tail gaps, choose \(k_n\uparrow\infty\) and put
\[
a_{n+1}=(1-t_n)a_n+t_ns_{k_n},\qquad
t_n=\frac{\eta}{\tau(s_{k_n}-a_n)}\in[\eta,1].
\]
Positive homogeneity gives \(\tau(a_{n+1}-a_n)=\eta\). Every upper bound of \(s_n\) bounds \(a_n\). Conversely, repeated convex interpolation toward any fixed \(s_j\), with residual coefficient at most \((1-\eta)^r\), shows every upper bound of \(a_n\) bounds \(s_j\). Thus lack of a supremum is preserved.

They also reconstructed bounded quasitrace-Cauchy gluing, **using standard finite-\(\mathrm{AW}^*\) continuous-dimension, polar-decomposition, and matrix-stability facts**: fast spectral cutoffs produce projections \(e_k\uparrow1\) on which suitable subsequence columns converge in norm. Compatible bounded columns glue through the join of their graph projections in \(M_2(M)\). A uniform graph-angle bound passes to that join by rank continuity, yielding a bounded graph operator in \(M\). Positivity and order pass to the limit.

Subject to that standard background, these arguments identify the requested assertion with **monotone sequential completeness of finite \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-factors**. They proved the surrounding reduction, not that structural theorem. No reliable theorem statement or citation establishing the missing step was located.

## Other reusable auxiliary results

The final new lemma was independently checked analytically:

> If \(0\le a\le b\) in an \(\mathrm{AW}^*\)-algebra and \(a\ne b\), then either \(\|b\|>\|a\|\), or some rational \(t>0\), with \(q_t=1_{(-\infty,t)}(a)\), satisfies  
> \[
> \|q_tbq_t\|>\|q_taq_t\|.
> \]

For the contrapositive, set \(c=b-a\). Equal compression norms imply
\(q_tcq_t\le(t-a)q_t\). For a state \(\psi\), the positive functional
\[
f\mapsto\psi(c^{1/2}f(a)c^{1/2})
\]
defines a scalar Riesz measure \(\mu\). Continuous regularizers yield
\[
\int_{s<t}(t-s)^{-1}\,d\mu(s)\le1
\]
for rational \(t\), hence all \(t>0\) by lower semicontinuity. Tonelli forces \(\mu=0\), and therefore \(c=0\). This avoids assuming states are normal on spectral projections. Its application to an \(\omega_1\)-chain stalled because the detecting projections change with the reference element.

Other proved ingredients include finite-spectrum positive directional derivatives via Kato block diagonalization and pinching; a pinching-support rank identity; weighted projection-join estimates; a uniformly invertible contraction-product estimate for Bessel projections; and quasitracial-ultraproduct constructions from standard dimension theory. None closes exhaustion.

## Failed routes and genuine obstructions

* Operator square superadditivity is false: for two explicit \(2\times2\) projections \(A,C\), \(\det(AC+CA)=-1/4\).
* Real rank zero and stable rank one do **not** imply hyponormal elements are normal. Weighted truncated shifts in \(\prod M_N/\bigoplus M_N\) give a nonnormal hyponormal element. Its defect is quasitrace-null, so this does not refute faithful-quasitrace rigidity.
* Not every conditional expectation onto a masa is faithful, even in the hyperfinite \(\mathrm{II}_1\) factor. They constructed a nonfaithful expectation using tail tensor projections and a central weak-* cluster state. Existence of **some** faithful expectation remained unproved.
* Projection countable-chain conditions do not imply weak-* ccc of the state space: an uncountable Clifford-factor example disproves that shortcut.
* Dimension-only packing inequalities admit the scalar model \(d(C)=\max(0,1-1/C)\); extensive exact checks show those inequalities alone cannot finish.
* Uniform strict order-monotonicity of faithful quasitraces, general hyponormal rigidity, finite-cotype bounds, and stable normality of infinite amplifications all remained unsupported inputs.

## Established results

The team did **not** prove the prescribed answer \(\mathcal G=(0,\tfrac12)\). They established
\[
\boxed{\mathcal G\subseteq(0,\tfrac12]}
\]
and that \(\mathcal G\) is downward closed. They constructed no witness for any positive \(\eta\), and did not exclude \(\eta=\tfrac12\). Nothing they established contradicts the prescribed answer.

### 1. Quasitrace monotonicity and the upper bound

The final argument derives the needed monotonicity directly from standard AW\(^*\) spectral projections and polar decomposition, without assuming additivity on noncommuting positive elements.

For \(0\le x\le y\), set
\[
p=1_{(t+\varepsilon,\infty)}(x),\qquad
r=1_{(t,\infty)}(y).
\]
Then \(p\wedge(1-r)=0\): compression to a nonzero common subprojection would give \(x\ge(t+\varepsilon)1\) and \(y\le t1\), contradicting \(x\le y\). The polar decomposition of \(rp\) therefore makes \(p\) Murray–von Neumann equivalent to a subprojection of \(r\). Quasitrace invariance under equivalence and additivity on orthogonal projections give
\[
\tau(p)\le\tau(r).
\]
Spectral-step approximation, or integration of spectral tails followed by \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), yields \(\tau(x)\le\tau(y)\).

Writing \(b_n=a_{n+1}-a_n\), the inequalities
\[
b_{n-1}\le a_n,\qquad b_n\le1-a_n
\]
give, for \(n\ge1\),
\[
\eta\le\tau(a_n)\le1-\eta.
\]
Here \(\tau(1-a_n)=1-\tau(a_n)\) uses only linearity in the abelian algebra generated by \(a_n,1\). Thus \(\eta\le\tfrac12\). At equality, necessarily \(\tau(a_n)=\tfrac12\) for every \(n\ge1\).

### 2. Downward closure

If a sequence witnesses \(\eta_0\), then for \(0<\eta\le\eta_0\),
\[
c_n=(\eta/\eta_0)a_n
\]
witnesses \(\eta\). Homogeneity gives the required increments, and a least upper bound for \((c_n)\) would scale back to one for \((a_n)\).

Consequently, \(\mathcal G\) is either empty or an initial positive interval, with supremum at most \(\tfrac12\). This proves neither nonemptiness nor the location or inclusion of its endpoint.

### 3. Every witness requires a nontracial quasitrace

This is the central obstruction they identified. If \(\tau\) were additive on positive elements, then
\[
N\eta=\tau(a_N)-\tau(a_0)\le1,
\]
impossible for \(N>1/\eta\). Equivalently, positive additivity applied to
\[
1=a_0+\sum_{n<N}b_n+(1-a_N)
\]
would give \(1\ge N\eta\).

More quantitatively, defining
\[
D_n=\tau(a_{n+1})-\tau(a_n)-\eta,
\]
one has
\[
\sum_{n<N}D_n=\tau(a_N)-\tau(a_0)-N\eta\le1-N\eta.
\]
Since \(t_n=\tau(a_n)\) is increasing and bounded, \(t_{n+1}-t_n\to0\), so \(D_n\to-\eta\). A witness requires persistent negative additivity defects.

They also explained why finite von Neumann factors cannot supply examples. On matrix algebras, equivalence of rank-one projections and spectral decomposition force every normalized quasitrace to be normalized trace. In a type \(\mathrm{II}_1\) von Neumann factor, projection equivalence and comparison with rational-dimension projections determine quasitrace values on projections; spectral approximation then determines it on self-adjoint elements. Thus a witness would be a non-von-Neumann finite AW\(^*\)-factor, necessarily type \(\mathrm{II}_1\), and would contradict Kaplansky’s AW\(^*\)-factor conjecture. This is an implication, **not a contradiction of the problem’s asserted answer**.

## Additional reductions and exploratory work

For \(0<\delta<\eta\), spectral projections
\[
p_n=1_{(\delta,\infty)}(b_n)
\]
satisfy
\[
\sum_{n<N}p_n\le\delta^{-1}1,\qquad
\tau(p_n)\ge\frac{\eta-\delta}{1-\delta}>0.
\]
Thus a witness would produce infinitely many uniformly positive-quasitrace projections with bounded partial sums. They did not rule this out or construct it.

They investigated
\[
K=\sup\left\{\sum_i\tau(c_i):c_i\ge0,\ \sum_i c_i\le1\right\}.
\]
For finite \(K\), they gave a compactness/separation proof of a dominating state \(\phi\) with \(\tau(c)\le K\phi(c)\) for all \(c\ge0\). Their proposed continuation—using GNS strong* approximation and quasitracial metric completion to deduce that \(\tau\) is a trace—remained dependent on completion and continuity machinery not fully verified in the record. # Audit: normal AW* versus monotone completion

This note does NOT claim normal AW* implies monotone completeness.
No verified theorem or counterexample settling that implication was
identified offline. The following exact lemmas delimit the proposed route.

## 1. Positive congruence preserves existing projection suprema
If p=sup p_i in M_sa and x>=0, then x p x=sup x p_i x.
For invertible x this is an order isomorphism. For general x use x+delta,
whose products differ uniformly from those for x by O(delta), and pass to
the norm-closed positive cone.

## 2. Normality gives the correct ambient supremum for commuting positives
Let a_i increase in one masa, with supremum a there. Suppose b>=a_i.
For delta>0 set p_delta=1_[delta,infinity)(a). In the p_delta corner,
a is invertible; set c_i=p_delta a_i a^{-1} p_delta. For epsilon>0 the
high spectral projections r_i=1_[1-epsilon,1](c_i) increase to p_delta.
We have b>=a_i>=(1-epsilon)a^{1/2}r_i a^{1/2}. Projection normality
and Lemma 1 imply b>=(1-epsilon)a p_delta. Let epsilon go to zero,
then delta go to zero in norm, obtaining b>=a. This only treats a
commuting family, and does not construct a supremum for noncommuting a_i.

## 3. No proper positive-order-dense monotone-complete extension of an AW*
Let M be AW* and B a monotone-complete C* algebra containing M as a
unital C* subalgebra. Assume every nonzero b in B_+ dominates a nonzero
member of M_+. Then B=M.

First, old positive carriers are preserved. For a in M_+, let
p=supp_M(a), q=supp_B(a); q<=p. If p-q is nonzero, order density gives
0!=c in M_+ with c<=p-q. Then ac=0, so the AW right-annihilator property
implies c=(1-p)c. But c<=p implies c=pc, a contradiction. Hence p=q.

Every nonzero projection of B now dominates a nonzero projection of M:
choose old positive c below it and take c's (preserved) carrier.
For q in Proj(B), put p=sup_M{r in Proj(M):r<=q}. To see p<=q without
assuming join preservation, first let s=sup_B of this family, so s<=p.
If p-s were nonzero, projection order density would give old r<=p-s;
then p-r is an old upper bound of the family smaller than p. Thus s=p,
and p<=q. If q-p were nonzero, old r<=q-p contradicts the definition
of p. Consequently every projection of B lies in M. Spectral finite-step
approximation in the monotone-complete algebra B and norm-closedness of
M imply B=M.

Thus a putative 'regular monotone completion' that is positive-order-dense
would already prove the desired completeness (indeed for all AW* algebras).
One must not assume this density from injective-envelope essentiality:
operator-system essentiality is not positive order density. Normality of
the original AW* alone has not been shown here to supply such an extension.

## 4. Stable-normality/Naimark route remains conditional
An infinite AW* amplification preserving M as a finite corner, together
with projection normality in that amplification, would let a Naimark
dilation turn a bounded increasing positive sequence into increasing
projections and recover its supremum by corner compression. The missing
step is stable normality (and a legitimate corner-preserving amplification),
not finite-corner normality. For p_n increasing to p, finite e<=p need
not satisfy e meet p_n increasing to e; this fails even for rank-one e
and finite-coordinate p_n in B(l2). Therefore finite continuous dimension
cannot justify the required compression convergence e p_n e by this meet
argument.

# Countable spectral-compression norm detection

## Statement
Let A be a unital AW*-algebra and 0 <= a <= b in A. For each positive
rational t let q_t be the carrier projection of (t*1-a)_+; this is the
spectral cut 1_{(-infinity,t)}(a). If

    ||q_t b q_t|| = ||q_t a q_t||   for every positive rational t,

then b=a. Thus a strict ordered increase is detected by one of this
countable family of compression norms. No quasitrace or finiteness is used.

## Proof
Put c=b-a >= 0 and R=||a||. For rational t>R, q_t=1, so the hypothesis
implies ||b||=R and hence b<=R*1. For every positive rational t, positivity
and the norm hypothesis imply

    q_t b q_t <= ||q_t a q_t|| q_t <= t q_t,
    q_t c q_t <= (t*1-a) q_t.                         (1)

Suppose c is nonzero. Choose a state psi with psi(c)>0. The positive linear
functional f -> psi(c^(1/2) f(a) c^(1/2)) on C(sigma(a)) has a finite positive
Radon representing measure mu, with total mass psi(c)>0. This is a measure
on the ordinary compact spectrum; we do NOT identify its values on Borel
sets with psi evaluated on AW* spectral projections.

Fix positive rational t and positive integer n. For s in sigma(a) write
r=(t-s)_+ and define

    f_n(s) = r/(r+1/n)^2,     g_n(s)=sqrt(f_n(s)).

These are continuous functions, q_t g_n(a)=g_n(a), and
0 <= (t-s) f_n(s) <= 1. Sandwiching (1) by g_n(a) gives

    0 <= g_n(a) c g_n(a) <= 1.

The C*-identity ||z*z||=||zz*||, applied to z=c^(1/2)g_n(a), consequently gives

    0 <= c^(1/2) f_n(a) c^(1/2) <= 1.

Apply psi. As n increases, f_n(s) increases pointwise to
1_{s<t}/(t-s), with value zero when s=t. Monotone convergence yields

    H(t) := integral_{s<t} dmu(s)/(t-s) <= 1            (2)

for positive rational t. For fixed s, the function of t equal to 0 for
t<=s and 1/(t-s) for t>s is nonnegative and lower semicontinuous. Fatou's
lemma therefore makes H lower semicontinuous on (0,infinity). Approaching
any t>0 by positive rationals in (2) proves H(t)<=1 for every t>0.

Every inner integral is infinite, including s=R. Since mu has positive
